reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: An inflammatory syndrome of the medial temporal lobes presenting subacutely with short-term memory loss, confusion, psychiatric change, and seizures
It may be paraneoplastic (driven by an underlying cancer) or a primary autoimmune process, and identifying the antibody helps predict the association with tumour

Antibodies to intracellular antigens (e.g. Hu, Ma2) carry a strong cancer association and respond less well to immunotherapy, whereas surface-antigen antibodies (e.g. LGI1, NMDA receptor, GABA-B) often respond better
LGI1 antibody encephalitis characteristically causes faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatraemia
NMDA-receptor encephalitis often affects younger patients with psychiatric onset, movement disorders, autonomic instability, and reduced consciousness, and is associated with ovarian teratoma
Brain MRI typically shows increased T2/FLAIR signal in the medial temporal lobes, and CSF may show a lymphocytic pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands
A thorough search for an occult malignancy is essential and may need repeating over time if initial screening is negative
Early immunotherapy and treatment of any underlying tumour improve outcome, so prompt recognition matters
reference.pathophysiology: Limbic encephalitis results from an immune attack, often antibody-mediated, directed at neuronal antigens concentrated in the limbic system, particularly the hippocampi and amygdalae. In paraneoplastic disease, a systemic tumour expresses neuronal antigens that trigger a cross-reactive immune response; antibodies against intracellular antigens mark a T-cell-mediated, less reversible process, whereas antibodies against neuronal surface proteins (such as NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, and GABA-B receptor) are considered directly pathogenic and more treatment-responsive. Inflammation of limbic structures produces the memory, behavioural, and seizure manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex and other viral encephalitis
Status epilepticus and other seizure disorders
Rapidly progressive dementia including prion disease
CNS lymphoma or other neoplastic infiltration
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid neuronal antibody panels (surface and intracellular antigens)
Brain MRI focused on the medial temporal lobes
Lumbar puncture for cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, and to exclude infection
EEG for seizures and encephalopathic patterns
Whole-body CT and FDG-PET to search for an underlying malignancy, with repeat surveillance if negative
Age- and antibody-directed tumour screening (e.g. pelvic imaging for ovarian teratoma in NMDA-receptor disease)
redFlags: Subacute encephalopathy warrants urgent workup for autoimmune and paraneoplastic causes alongside exclusion of infective encephalitis
Positive onconeural or surface antibodies mandate a directed and, if negative, repeated search for occult cancer
Refractory seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent management
Autonomic instability or reduced consciousness (notably in NMDA-receptor encephalitis) needing intensive monitoring
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the antibody and cause: surface-antigen syndromes and prompt immunotherapy often allow substantial recovery, whereas classic paraneoplastic encephalitis with intracellular-antigen antibodies tends to respond poorly and is dominated by the underlying malignancy.
pitfalls: Failing to start empirical aciclovir while herpes simplex encephalitis remains possible
Not searching thoroughly, or repeatedly, for an occult tumour after a negative initial screen
Missing faciobrachial dystonic seizures as a treatable clue to LGI1 antibody disease
Attributing early psychiatric presentations solely to a primary psychiatric disorder
Delaying immunotherapy while awaiting antibody results in a clinically compatible case
management: Institute first-line immunotherapy promptly with high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and/or plasma exchange, which is most effective in the surface-antigen antibody syndromes
Escalate to second-line immunotherapy such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide for refractory, severe or relapsing disease
Search for and treat any underlying malignancy, for example resection of an ovarian teratoma in NMDA-receptor disease, which is central to controlling paraneoplastic forms
Control seizures, including faciobrachial dystonic seizures in LGI1 disease, with antiseizure medication

Provide supportive and symptomatic care, managing psychiatric disturbance, movement disorder and autonomic instability, with intensive care and airway support for reduced consciousness in NMDA-receptor disease
Correct associated hyponatraemia, characteristic of LGI1 antibody disease
Undertake surveillance tumour imaging when the initial screen is negative, as the malignancy may only declare itself later
Refer for neurorehabilitation and neuropsychological support to aid cognitive and functional recovery
